ResearchDossier.topic: advent calendars started as chalk marks
ResearchDossier.summary: Early advent counting in Germany included 24 chalk marks on a wall or door, one wiped off each day. The first documented advent calendar dates from 1839. Munich publisher Gerhard Lang, whose mother sewed 24 small baked goods onto cardboard for him each Advent, printed 'Im Lande des Christkinds' in 1903. Calendars with little opening windows spread after 1920. The first chocolate-filled advent calendar went on sale in 1958.

Script.headline: Advent Calendars Began as Chalk
Script.cta: Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.

lines.text: Before the chocolate, advent calendars were chalk marks on a door.
Some German families drew 24 lines, and the kids wiped one away each day.
The first documented advent calendar dates back to 1839.
Then a boy named Gerhard Lang got a tastier version. His mother sewed 24 little biscuits onto cardboard.
He grew up to be a publisher. And in 1903, in Munich, he printed one.
After 1920, calendars with little doors took off.
And in 1958, someone finally put chocolate behind them.
Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.

PublishCopy.title: Advent calendars started as chalk marks on a door
PublishCopy.description:
Before the chocolate, advent calendars were chalk marks on a door.
Some German families drew 24 lines and wiped one away each day. Gerhard Lang's mother sewed 24 biscuits onto cardboard for him; in 1903 he printed one in Munich. Little doors took off after 1920, and chocolate arrived in 1958.
